related_questions.question: What are the new CPR guidelines?

text_blocks.snippet: The latest CPR guidelines, primarily from the American Heart Association (AHA), emphasize a faster rate and deeper chest compressions, with a shift to Hands-Only CPR for untrained lay rescuers. The sequence has changed from ABC (Airway, Breathing, Chest compressions) to CAB (Chest compressions, Airway, Breathing). For adults and children, the recommended compression rate is 100-120 per minute, with a depth of at least 2 inches (5-6 cm). Hands-Only CPR is recommended for untrained individuals.
snippet_highlighted_words: emphasize a faster rate and deeper chest compressions, with a shift to Hands-Only CPR for untrained lay rescuers

list.title: Chest Compressions:
list.snippet: The core of CPR remains chest compressions. Push hard and fast in the center of the chest, ensuring full chest recoil between compressions. The recommended depth is at least 2 inches for adults and children, and 1.5 inches for infants.

list.title: Compression Rate:
list.snippet: Aim for 100-120 compressions per minute. Healthdirect says to "push swiftly and forcefully".

list.title: CAB Sequence:
list.snippet: For adults and children, the initial step is chest compressions, followed by airway management (head tilt, chin lift) and rescue breaths.

list.title: Hands-Only CPR:
list.snippet: For untrained individuals, the focus should be on continuous chest compressions until emergency help arrives.

list.title: Ventilation:
list.snippet: When trained, rescuers should provide 2 rescue breaths after every 30 compressions for adults and children (30:2 ratio). For infants and children with two or more rescuers, the ratio is 15:2.

list.title: AED:
list.snippet: If an Automated External Defibrillator (AED) is available, it should be used as quickly as possible.

list.title: Minimizing Interruptions:
list.snippet: A key aspect of high-quality CPR is minimizing interruptions to chest compressions.

list.title: No need to check pulse:
list.snippet: The updated guidelines state not to check for a pulse during CPR.

list.title: Continue CPR until:
list.snippet: Emergency help arrives, the person shows signs of life, or the rescuer is too exhausted to continue, according to CPR Certification Plano.
